Data Wrangling

We’ll pick up more-or-less where we left off with the V-DEM data and discuss a couple of ways we could use it to analyze opportunity structures and contention. But first, we’ll need to do a little data wrangling to get things in a proper working order.

Setup

We’ve got three new packages that we’ll use in this class, so you can go ahead and run this chunk to install those:

install.packages("wbstats")
install.packages('ggcorrplot')
install.packages('countrycode')

Then run the code below to load the libraries and data:

library(tidyverse)
library(wbstats)
library(countrycode)
library(ggcorrplot)
vdem<-vdemdata::vdem
codebook<-vdemdata::codebook

Here’s a (slightly modified) list of the variables that you all selected from the previous class, we’ll use these for the example data:

# a list of columns to use in this analysis:

cols <- c(
  'country_name',  #
  'year',          #
  'COWcode',       # numeric country ID
  'e_regionpol_6C',# 6 category political/geographic region
  'v2mecenefm',    # government censorship of media
  'v2csreprss',    # civil society repression
  'v2x_elecreg',   # Does the country have elections? 1 = yes, 0 = no
  'v2eldonate',    # disclosure of campaign donations
  'v2elvaptrn',    # % of voting age population who cast a vote 
  'v2x_cspart',    # index of civil society participation
  'v2cagenmob',    # mass mobilization
  'v2csreprss',    # civil society repression
  'v2elparlel',    # lower chamber electoral system (categorical)
  'v2jucomp',      # index of judicial constraints on executive
  'v2psbars',      # barriers to forming a party
  'v2mebias',      # is there media bias against opposition parties?
  'v2asuffrage',   # de-facto % of adults with suffrage
  'v2elfrfair',    # would you consider this national election to be free and fair?
  'v2clstown',     # State ownership of economy
  'v2svstterr',    # State effective control of territory
  'v2smgovshut',   # State shuts down internet
  'v2psnatpar'     # unified party control of govt.
)



# get the codebook entries for the selected columns
selected_codes<-codebook|>
  filter(tag %in% cols)

Subsetting, recoding, and filling

While not an absolute necessity, we can simplify our analyses a bit by getting rid of a lot of the columns in the V-DEM data set that we won’t be using.

select will retrieve only specific columns from a data frame. For instance, I could use this expression to retrieve the country_name and year columns:

vdem|>
  select(country_name, year)|>
  slice_head(n=5)
country_name year
Mexico 1789
Mexico 1790
Mexico 1791
Mexico 1792
Mexico 1793

There are a number of “helper” functions that we can used with select to quickly select multiple columns without having to write out the names of each one. For instance: all_of(x) would retrieve all columns that are present in the character vector “x”. So the code below will give us a data frame containing only the columns from the cols vector we made above:

vdem_select <- vdem |>
  # this selects only colums in "cols"
  select(all_of(cols)) 

vdem_select|>slice_head(n=5)
country_name year COWcode e_regionpol_6C v2mecenefm v2csreprss v2x_elecreg v2eldonate v2elvaptrn v2x_cspart v2cagenmob v2elparlel v2jucomp v2psbars v2mebias v2asuffrage v2elfrfair v2clstown v2svstterr v2smgovshut v2psnatpar
Mexico 1789 70 2 NA -1.516 0 -1.492 NA 0.031 NA NA -0.358 -2.537 -1.781 NA NA -0.171 NA NA NA
Mexico 1790 70 2 NA -1.516 0 -1.492 NA 0.031 NA NA -0.358 -2.537 -1.781 NA NA -0.171 NA NA NA
Mexico 1791 70 2 NA -1.516 0 -1.492 NA 0.031 NA NA -0.358 -2.537 -1.781 NA NA -0.171 NA NA NA
Mexico 1792 70 2 NA -1.516 0 -1.492 NA 0.031 NA NA -0.358 -2.537 -1.781 NA NA -0.171 NA NA NA
Mexico 1793 70 2 NA -1.516 0 -1.492 NA 0.031 NA NA -0.358 -2.537 -1.781 NA NA -0.171 NA NA NA

Recoding

The next thing I might want to do here is re-code some of these categorical variables. There are three variables in our selections that have numeric values in the data that need to be mapped on to categorical labels: v2elparlel, v2x_elecreg, e_regionpol_6C:

vdem_select|>
  filter(year==2015)|>
  select(country_name, year, v2elparlel, v2x_elecreg, e_regionpol_6C)|>
  slice_head(n=5)
country_name year v2elparlel v2x_elecreg e_regionpol_6C
Mexico 2015 2 1 2
Suriname 2015 1 1 2
Sweden 2015 NA 1 5
Switzerland 2015 1 1 5
Ghana 2015 NA 1 4

I’ll need to consult the codebook to get a sense of what categories go with each numeric value, then I’ll need to use the factor function to give a text label to each value.

vdem_select<-vdem_select|>
  mutate(
    v2elparlel = factor(
      v2elparlel,
      levels = c(0, 1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Majoritarian", "Proportional", "Mixed", "Other")
    ), 
    # recoding the electoral regime variable
    v2x_elecreg = factor(
      v2x_elecreg,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("No", "Yes")
      ), 
    e_regionpol_6C  = factor(
      e_regionpol_6C,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), 
      labels = c(
        "E. Europe/Central Asia",
        "Latin America/Caribbean",
        "Middle East/North Africa",
        "Sub-Saharan Africa",
        "W. Europe/N. America",
        "Asia and Pacific"
      )
    )
   
  )

# comparing the results:
vdem_select|>
  filter(year==2015)|>
  select(country_name, year, v2elparlel, v2x_elecreg, e_regionpol_6C)|>
  slice_head(n=5)
country_name year v2elparlel v2x_elecreg e_regionpol_6C
Mexico 2015 Mixed Yes Latin America/Caribbean
Suriname 2015 Proportional Yes Latin America/Caribbean
Sweden 2015 NA Yes W. Europe/N. America
Switzerland 2015 Proportional Yes W. Europe/N. America
Ghana 2015 NA Yes Sub-Saharan Africa

Filling and mutating

Finally, you might notice that a lot of election-related variables are missing for most years in the data:

vdem_select|>
  filter(year>2015)|>
  select(country_name, year, v2elvaptrn, v2elparlel)|>
  slice_head(n=10)
country_name year v2elvaptrn v2elparlel
Mexico 2016 NA NA
Mexico 2017 NA NA
Mexico 2018 65.62 Mixed
Mexico 2019 NA NA
Mexico 2020 NA NA
Mexico 2021 54.52 Mixed
Mexico 2022 NA NA
Mexico 2023 NA NA
Suriname 2016 NA NA
Suriname 2017 NA NA

That’s because many of these variables are specific to a single election, and countries generally don’t have a national election every single year. When it comes to v2elparlel (the lower chamber electoral system) we don’t necessarily expect this to change dramatically from one election to the next. So it might make sense to just carry forward the value from the most recent election to the missing data for each subsequent year.

We can do this with the fill function, which will just take a variable name and a .direction argument to control how values are carried forward:

vdem_select|>
  filter(year>2015)|>
  select(country_name, year,v2elparlel)|>
  # making a copy of v2elparlel, so I can compare the results:
  mutate(most_recent_election_type = v2elparlel)|>
  fill(most_recent_election_type, .direction='down')|>
  slice_head(n=10)
country_name year v2elparlel most_recent_election_type
Mexico 2016 NA NA
Mexico 2017 NA NA
Mexico 2018 Mixed Mixed
Mexico 2019 NA Mixed
Mexico 2020 NA Mixed
Mexico 2021 Mixed Mixed
Mexico 2022 NA Mixed
Mexico 2023 NA Mixed
Suriname 2016 NA Mixed
Suriname 2017 NA Mixed

However! I want to be careful here, because it makes sense to fill missing values this way within a single country, but it doesn’t make sense to fill in Suriname’s values with values from Mexico’s most recent election.

So, in this case, I’ll want to pair fill with a group_by statement to ensure the filling only occurs within countries:

vdem_select|>
  filter(year>2015)|>
  select(country_name, year,v2elparlel)|>
  # making a copy of v2elparlel, so I can compare the results:
  mutate(most_recent_election_type = v2elparlel)|>
  # grouping the data by country
  group_by(country_name)|>
  # filling in election values
  fill(most_recent_election_type, .direction='down')|>
  # ungrouping the data
  ungroup()|>
  slice_head(n=10)
country_name year v2elparlel most_recent_election_type
Mexico 2016 NA NA
Mexico 2017 NA NA
Mexico 2018 Mixed Mixed
Mexico 2019 NA Mixed
Mexico 2020 NA Mixed
Mexico 2021 Mixed Mixed
Mexico 2022 NA Mixed
Mexico 2023 NA Mixed
Suriname 2016 NA NA
Suriname 2017 NA NA

I’ll apply this function to the data set and assign the result to a new data frame called vdem_filled.

vdem_filled<-vdem_select|>
  filter(year>2015)|>
  # making a copy of v2elparlel, so I can compare the results:
  mutate(most_recent_election_type = v2elparlel)|>
  # grouping the data by country
  group_by(country_name)|>
  # filling in election values
  fill(most_recent_election_type, .direction='down')|>
  # ungrouping the data
  ungroup()
  
vdem_filled|>
  slice_head(n= 10)
country_name year COWcode e_regionpol_6C v2mecenefm v2csreprss v2x_elecreg v2eldonate v2elvaptrn v2x_cspart v2cagenmob v2elparlel v2jucomp v2psbars v2mebias v2asuffrage v2elfrfair v2clstown v2svstterr v2smgovshut v2psnatpar most_recent_election_type
Mexico 2016 70 Latin America/Caribbean 1.111 1.369 Yes 1.870 NA 0.641 0.579 NA 0.357 1.258 2.416 100 1.059 1.455 86.900 1.410 0.697 NA
Mexico 2017 70 Latin America/Caribbean 0.758 1.242 Yes 1.844 NA 0.687 0.780 NA 0.357 1.258 1.546 100 1.059 1.267 86.600 1.825 0.697 NA
Mexico 2018 70 Latin America/Caribbean 1.052 1.384 Yes 2.008 65.62 0.654 0.414 Mixed 0.357 1.258 1.910 100 1.514 0.961 87.375 1.450 1.267 Mixed
Mexico 2019 70 Latin America/Caribbean 0.144 1.279 Yes 2.008 NA 0.557 0.862 NA 0.570 1.398 1.665 100 1.514 0.897 87.375 1.450 1.006 Mixed
Mexico 2020 70 Latin America/Caribbean -0.108 0.998 Yes 2.062 NA 0.568 0.064 NA 0.381 1.398 1.838 100 1.514 0.869 86.500 1.828 1.006 Mixed
Mexico 2021 70 Latin America/Caribbean -0.021 0.733 Yes 2.036 54.52 0.523 -0.425 Mixed -0.015 1.343 2.471 100 0.957 0.869 89.143 1.828 0.974 Mixed
Mexico 2022 70 Latin America/Caribbean -0.102 0.713 Yes 1.921 NA 0.479 0.238 NA -0.015 1.368 1.845 100 0.957 0.869 91.167 1.828 0.974 Mixed
Mexico 2023 70 Latin America/Caribbean -0.102 0.713 Yes 1.732 NA 0.512 0.517 NA -0.355 1.368 1.610 100 0.957 0.893 91.333 1.828 0.974 Mixed
Suriname 2016 115 Latin America/Caribbean 1.450 2.490 Yes -0.530 NA 0.753 -1.103 NA 1.427 2.120 1.625 100 1.381 -0.274 79.000 1.752 -0.436 NA
Suriname 2017 115 Latin America/Caribbean 1.064 1.853 Yes -0.530 NA 0.753 -1.103 NA 1.427 2.120 1.625 100 1.381 -0.274 79.000 1.752 -0.436 NA

We could apply this same “filling” process to the voter turnout measure v2elvaptrn, but you might notice an odd pattern here as well. The problem is probably easiest to spot if we look at a familiar example, so we’ll check out the voter turnout for the US after 1945:

vdem_select|>
  filter(year>=1945)|>
  filter(country_name == "United States of America")|>
  select(country_name, year, v2elvaptrn)|>
  drop_na()|>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=v2elvaptrn, group=1)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line()

Given this clear pattern of variability across election types, we probably don’t want to just “fill” the missing values from the most recent election here, because that would mean that some countries would get arbitrarily lower values depending on what kind of election they had most recently.

Instead, we might want to do something like take the highest turnout in the last 10 years, or the average turnout across multiple cycles, to get a sense of each country’s voter turnout patterns. Instead of using “fill” here, we could use group_by with mutate to calculate a maximum values within each country.

(Note that we already filtered vdem_filled to only contain values from 2015 onward. If we hadn’t done this, we would get the highest turnout election in the entire history of a given country, which probably wouldn’t make sense)

vdem_filled<-vdem_filled|>
  group_by(country_name)|>
  mutate(highest_turnout = max(v2elvaptrn, na.rm=T))|>
  # ungrouping the data
  ungroup()

As a final step, we’re going to restrict our analysis to 2023 data, which is the most recent year where these variables are available. But note that our filling and mutating has made it so that we actually have some values that have been filled down or aggregated from as early as 2015:

vdem_latest<-vdem_filled|>
  filter(year == 2023)

We’ll finish our data cleanup by dropping v2elvaptrn and v2elparlel (since we’ve already made more useable copies of these variables) and then creating vdem_no_missing by dropping any rows that having missing or non-finite values. We want to be careful using drop_na because we can end up arbitrarily dropping nearly all of our data, but since we want to use all of the selected columns in a potential analysis, we’re ultimately forced to get rid of some rows that don’t have the information we need. Luckily, this only requires us to get rid of a handful of rows:

vdem_no_missing<-
  vdem_latest|>
  select(-v2elvaptrn, -v2elparlel)|>
  drop_na()|>
  filter(!is.infinite(highest_turnout))

nrow(vdem_no_missing)
[1] 153
nrow(vdem_latest)
[1] 179

In case you got lost

Just in case you got lost in all that coding, you can click the button to see everything in one big chunk of code:

Code 
library(tidyverse)
library(wbstats)
library(countrycode)
library(ggcorrplot)
vdem<-vdemdata::vdem
codebook<-vdemdata::codebook

cols <- c(
  'country_name',  #
  'year',          #
  'COWcode',       # numeric country ID
  'e_regionpol_6C',# 6 category political/geographic region
  'v2mecenefm',    # government censorship of media
  'v2csreprss',    # civil society repression
  'v2x_elecreg',   # Does the country have elections? 1 = yes, 0 = no
  'v2eldonate',    # disclosure of campaign donations
  'v2elvaptrn',    # % of voting age population who cast a vote 
  'v2x_cspart',    # index of civil society participation
  'v2cagenmob',    # mass mobilization
  'v2csreprss',    # civil society repression
  'v2elparlel',    # lower chamber electoral system (categorical)
  'v2jucomp',      # index of judicial constraints on executive
  'v2psbars',      # barriers to forming a party
  'v2mebias',      # is there media bias against opposition parties?
  'v2asuffrage',   # de-facto % of adults with suffrage
  'v2elfrfair',    # would you consider this national election to be free and fair?
  'v2clstown',     # State ownership of economy
  'v2svstterr',    # State effective control of territory
  'v2smgovshut',   # State shuts down internet
  'v2psnatpar'     # unified party control of govt.
)

vdem_select <- vdem |>
  # this selects only colums in "cols"
  select(all_of(cols)) 

vdem_select<-vdem_select|>
  mutate(
    v2elparlel = factor(
      v2elparlel,
      levels = c(0, 1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Majoritarian", "Proportional", "Mixed", "Other")
    ), 
    # recoding the electoral regime variable
    v2x_elecreg = factor(
      v2x_elecreg,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("No", "Yes")
      ), 
    e_regionpol_6C  = factor(
      e_regionpol_6C,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), 
      labels = c(
        "E. Europe/Central Asia",
        "Latin America/Caribbean",
        "Middle East/North Africa",
        "Sub-Saharan Africa",
        "W. Europe/N. America",
        "Asia and Pacific"
      )
    )
   
  )



vdem_filled<-vdem_select|>
  filter(year>2015)|>
  # making a copy of v2elparlel, so I can compare the results:
  mutate(most_recent_election_type = v2elparlel)|>
  # grouping the data by country
  group_by(country_name)|>
  # filling in election values
  fill(most_recent_election_type, .direction='down')|>
  # ungrouping the data
  ungroup()
vdem_filled<-vdem_filled|>
  group_by(country_name)|>
  mutate(highest_turnout = max(v2elvaptrn, na.rm=T))|>
  # ungrouping the data
  ungroup()


# getting only 2023
vdem_latest<-vdem_filled|>
  filter(year == 2023)

# getting only non-missing values
vdem_no_missing<-
  vdem_latest|>
  select(-v2elvaptrn, -v2elparlel)|>
  drop_na()|>
  filter(!is.infinite(highest_turnout))

Visualizing the data and selecting similar cases

Now that you’ve got the data in a use-able format, we can go back to some questions from the previous class:

Question 1

The variable v2cagenmob is a variable that ranges from -4 to +4, with higher values indicating more mass mobilization in a given country-year and lower values indicating less. Use scatter plots and geom_smooth to summarize the relationship between mass mobilization and state repression of civil society organizations (v2csreprss). Briefly discuss your results.

# code

Question 2

Create some graphs that you could use to select some variables for a most similar systems design that attempts to identify why countries would have higher or lower levels of mass mobilization in 2023. For a most similar systems analysis, you’ll want to look for countries that are similar with respect to most of the predictors but have different outcomes. So think about setting up visuals that could make it feasible to identify countries that fit these criteria.

Joining and countrycoding

What if we want to incorporate additional information that’s not available from V-DEM in our analyses?

For instance, maybe I want to include GDP per capita and total population in my analyses. While the V-DEM data does include these values, they don’t appear to have them for 2023 yet, so there’s not a good way to include them in my results.

However, these variables are currently available from the World Bank for most countries, and there’s another R package called wbstats that we can use to easily retrieve this data:

Once you’ve loaded wbstats, you can search for variables by using the wb_search function.

wb_search("GDP per capita")|>
  slice_head(n=1)
indicator_id indicator indicator_desc
5.51.01.10.gdp Per capita GDP growth GDP per capita is the sum of gross value added by all resident producers in the economy plus any product taxes (less subsidies) not included in the valuation of output, divided by mid-year population. Growth is calculated from constant price GDP data in local currency. Sustained economic growth increases average incomes and is strongly linked to poverty reduction. GDP per capita provides a basic measure of the value of output per person, which is an indirect indicator of per capita income. Growth in GDP and GDP per capita are considered broad measures of economic growth.

Then, you can run the code below to return GDP per capita and total population for the year 2023:

country_data <- wb_data(
  indicator = c('NY.GDP.PCAP.CD', "SP.POP.TOTL"),
  country = 'countries_only',
  start_date = 2023,
  end_date = 2023
)

country_data|>
  slice_head(n=4)
iso2c iso3c country date NY.GDP.PCAP.CD SP.POP.TOTL
AW ABW Aruba 2023 33984.7906 107359
AF AFG Afghanistan 2023 413.7579 41454761
AO AGO Angola 2023 2309.5341 36749906
AL ALB Albania 2023 8575.1713 2745972

However, we have another problem here: how do we combine the world bank data with our vdem data? To do this, we’ll need to use a “join” operation that combines “data set x” and “data set y” based on matching values in specific columns.

Here’s an example of that process using some example data from the dyplr package:

# data on band members
band_members
name band
Mick Stones
John Beatles
Paul Beatles 
# data on the instruments they play
band_instruments
name plays
John guitar
Paul bass
Keith guitar

And here’s how we might join those data sets using the name:

# joining band members and instruments based on the name:
full_join(x=band_members, y=band_instruments, by=join_by(name == name))
name band plays
Mick Stones NA
John Beatles guitar
Paul Beatles bass
Keith NA guitar

As is often the case, these two data sets don’t share exactly the same set of values, and there are some subtle differences in how we might handle these mismatches:

  • Left-join
  • Right-join
  • Inner-Join
  • Full-join

All rows in X that have matching keys in Y

left_join(x=band_members, y=band_instruments, by=join_by(name == name))
name band plays
Mick Stones NA
John Beatles guitar
Paul Beatles bass

All rows in Y that have matching keys in x

right_join(x=band_members, y=band_instruments, by=join_by(name == name))
name band plays
John Beatles guitar
Paul Beatles bass
Keith NA guitar

Only rows with matching keys in x and y:

inner_join(x=band_members, y=band_instruments, by=join_by(name == name))
name band plays
John Beatles guitar
Paul Beatles bass

All rows in x and y

full_join(x=band_members, y=band_instruments, by=join_by(name == name))
name band plays
Mick Stones NA
John Beatles guitar
Paul Beatles bass
Keith NA guitar

For our purposes in the analysis below, it probably makes sense to use a left join that preserves all the rows in the V-DEM data and includes any matching rows from the world bank. So now we just need to identify a good join key. Intuitively, it seems like we could just do this using the country names, but the spelling of country names is often very inconsistent across different data sources.

Instead of joining these two data sets based on country names, we’ll usually want to use some kind of agreed-upon country ID codes.

The V-DEM data includes the COWcode variable for this purpose. COWcode is a 2 or 3 digits numeric country ID that comes from the Correlates of War project.

vdem_no_missing|>
  select(country_name, COWcode)|>
  distinct()|>
  slice_head(n=5)
country_name COWcode
Mexico 70
Suriname 115
Sweden 380
Switzerland 225
Ghana 452

The World Bank data also includes its own country IDs from the International Organization for Standardization (or ISO):

country_data|>
  select(country, iso3c)|>
  slice_head(n=5)
country iso3c
Aruba ABW
Afghanistan AFG
Angola AGO
Albania ALB
Andorra AND

Fortunately, there’s yet another R package, countrycode, that we can use to match up different country codeing schemes. The core function is just called “countrycode” and we just need to give it a variable along with a code to indicate its origin and a code to indicate the “destination” or new format.

In this case, we want to turn an ISO3C code into a numeric correlates of war code:

country_data$COWcode<-countrycode(country_data$iso3c, 
            origin='iso3c', 
            destination = 'cown'
            )


country_data|>
  select(country, iso3c, COWcode)|>
  slice_head(n=5)
country iso3c COWcode
Aruba ABW NA
Afghanistan AFG 700
Angola AGO 540
Albania ALB 339
Andorra AND 232

You’ll notice some values are missing here, but this is inevitable because different sources often disagree about the precise definition of a country.

Now that we’ve got matching COW codes in both data sets, we can perform our join:

vdem_joined<-inner_join(x=vdem_no_missing, 
                       y=country_data, 
                       by=join_by(COWcode == COWcode))

vdem_joined|>slice_head(n=5)

# code

Extra code: creating a correlation matrix

We can use correlation matrices to visualize the relationships between pairs of numeric variables. The base R function cor will create a correlation matrix from any data frame with only numeric columns, but the results tend to strain the eyes if you have more than a handful of variables included.

vdem_no_missing|>
  # drop year and country code
  select(-year, -COWcode)|>
  # select only numeric columns
  select(where(is.numeric))|>
  # get the first five, just for this example:
  select(1:5)|>
  # get the correlation matrix:
  cor()
           v2mecenefm v2csreprss v2eldonate v2x_cspart v2cagenmob
v2mecenefm  1.0000000  0.8651565  0.5457547  0.8278549  0.1413208
v2csreprss  0.8651565  1.0000000  0.5204968  0.8374947  0.1435644
v2eldonate  0.5457547  0.5204968  1.0000000  0.4870822  0.2412862
v2x_cspart  0.8278549  0.8374947  0.4870822  1.0000000  0.2512328
v2cagenmob  0.1413208  0.1435644  0.2412862  0.2512328  1.0000000

Fortunately, there are several custom R packages that can help us create an easy to read visualization for a correlation matrix. We’ll try using ggcorrplot for this one.

When reading the chart, note that the elements along the diagonal are all “1” because its the correlation of each variable with itself. Positive values (more red) represent positive correlations, negative values (more blue) indicate negative relationships, and values closer to 0 are weaker than values absolutely closer to -1 or +1:

correlations<-vdem_no_missing|>
  select(where(is.numeric))|>
  select(-year, -COWcode)|>
  cor()




# creating a visual for the correlation matrix
ggcorrplot(correlations,   
           hc.order = TRUE,      # groups together similar variables in the plot
           type = "full",        # shows the full square matrix
           lab = TRUE)           # displays the actual numeric value of the correlation coefficient

When reading a matrix like this, two questions you can ask are: “which variables are positively or negatively correlated with the outcome of interest?” and “which variables, if any, are so strongly correlated with each other than they’re basically redundant?” In some cases you might re-consider including variables that are highly correlated with each other in an analysis. Several V-DEM variables are actually aggregated indices created from combinations of other V-DEM variables, so you would definitely want to consider not including a variable that is already a component of another variable!
